newsitem.title: USA: Democrats under pressure in New Mexico race.
newsitem.headline: Democrats under pressure in New Mexico race.

text.p: U.N. Ambassador Bill Richardson's former New Mexico congressional seat goes up for grabs Tuesday with the Democrats facing a stiff challenge to hold the seat from Republicans and the Green Party.
Eric Serna, the front-running Democratic candidate, faced Republican Bill Redmond and Carol Miller of the Green Party in the special election in the Third Congressional District.
Richardson, a Democrat, held the House seat for 14 years before taking his present post of ambassador to the United Nations in February.

Although registered Democrats outnumber Republicans more than two-to-one in New Mexico's northernmost congressional district, Serna's campaign has been hit by questions over his political past and by Miller's ability to attract Democrats.
A poll in Friday's daily Santa Fe New Mexican gave Serna 39 percent of the vote, only eight points ahead of Redmond.
Miller had 12 percent and two minor party candidates picked up a combined 3 percent, with 15 percent of voters surveyed still undecided.
Republicans currently hold a 227-to-206 lead over Democrats in the House, with one independent who usually votes with the Democrats.
Analysts said Redmond, a Christian minister, could score a major upset if turnout is low, and if Miller draws enough of the liberal vote away from Serna.
"I think he has a chance," said Jose Garcia, a government professor at New Mexico State Univeristy. "The question is whether the Greens can detract enough votes to allow Redmond to win."
Members of Serna's campaign team said they were banking on winning decisive support from northern New Mexico's predominantly Hispanic mountain towns and villages.
The area has long been a Democratic stronghold, but internal disputes over the selection process which offered up Serna as the party candidate could hurt his cause.
"I think some Democrats will stay away. They feel excluded from the nomination process," said Richard Bank, an associate professor of political science at the College of Santa Fe.
Miller, a public health consultant, has drawn support from poor neighbourhoods with her promise to push for an expansion of budget health care clinics and education services.

While Redmond has benefitted from Miller's spoiler campaign and has even applauded her in campaign literature, some analysts think the Green Party candidate herself could pull off a big surprise and take second place by drawing support from some Republicans.
The conservative Albuquerque Journal endorsed Miller Sunday, saying she was the only bright spot "in one of the more depressing political races in recent memory."
The campaign has been one of constant mud slinging between Serna and Redmond.
Redmond has painted Serna as a corrupt politician, hammering on his alleged misuse of public money and political influence while acting chairman of New Mexico's State Corporation Commission.
Serna, in turn, has characterised Redmond as a right-wing extremist, intent on imposing an anti-abortion and anti-gun control agenda on northern New Mexico.
